title: Rav Huna bar Chiyya
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a disciple of Rav Yehuda. Thus [Sanhedrin 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.100a.4) relates that Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya were preparing coverings for Rav Yehuda’s scrolls. When they reached the Scroll of Esther, they said, “This one does not need a covering.” Rav Yehuda told them, “Even conduct like this appears disrespectful.” Rashi explains that they should have addressed their master in the form of a question.[^12]

In [Shabbat 47a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.47a.6), Levi bar Shmuel found Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiyya standing at the entrance to Rav Huna’s house. He asked them, “May one reassemble a tradesmen’s bed on Shabbat?” They answered, “It is permitted.” They subsequently came before Rav Yehuda, who forbade it. At the beginning of [Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.12.1.4), Rav Hamnuna ruled that the Exilarch could take apart a jointed table on Shabbat. Rav Huna bar Chiyya was with him. Rav Yehuda heard about it and said, “The person who issued that ruling has neither learned nor served the sages.” In [Yevamot 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.18a.3), Rav Huna bar Chiyya raises an objection to Rav Yehuda.

Perhaps he was also fortunate enough to see Shmuel and receive teachings from him. We repeatedly find “R' Huna bar Chiyya said in Shmuel’s name”: [Shabbat 51b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.51b.17), [Taanit 10a](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.10a.12), [Ketubot 79b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.79b.7), [Chullin 79a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.79a.2), [Niddah 39a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.39a.13) and [63b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.63b.3), and [Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.2.5.3). He also received a ruling of Shmuel through Rav Kahana, as in [Ketubot 101a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.101a.9).[^1]

He also received teachings from Rav Huna. In [Bava Batra 111a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.111a.9), Rav Huna bar Chiyya intended to act upon a ruling. Rav Nachman asked him, “What is this?” He replied, “For Rav Huna said in Rav’s name…” Rav Nachman asked, “Shall I send to him?” Rav Huna bar Chiyya became embarrassed. Rav Nachman then said to him, “Now that Rav Huna has died, have you become bold enough to oppose me?” This suggests that he was something of a colleague of Rav Nachman.[^2] From [Bava Kamma 116b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.116b.21-22), however, he appears to have been something of his pupil-colleague: Rav Yosef sat behind Rav Huna bar Chiyya, while Rav Huna bar Chiyya sat before Rav Nachman. Rav Huna bar Chiyya asked, “Is this ordinary law or a penalty?” Rav Nachman answered, “It is a mishnah…” After Rav Nachman left, Rav Yosef asked Rav Huna bar Chiyya, “What difference does it make whether it is ordinary law or a penalty?” He answered, “If it is ordinary law…” and so forth.

He married the daughter of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, a pupil-colleague of Rav, and received teachings from him as well. Thus in [Shabbat 156a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.156a.3) and [Chullin 93a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.93a.11), he told his son Levi, “This is what your mother’s father said in Rav’s name”—the reference being to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba. In [Bava Kamma 59b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.59b.6), too, Rav Huna bar Chiyya reports a teaching of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba. Their disagreement appears in [Shabbat 80b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.80b.2).
He also reported teachings in Ulla’s name, as in [Nedarim 56a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.56a.4).

His colleagues included all the leading scholars of the generation. Among them was Rabbi Abba I: [Moed Katan 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.26a.20-21) relates that, as they once sat together, an ostrich came and was about to swallow Rabbi Abba’s tefillin, and he rescued them. In [Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 3:7:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.7.11), the account is reversed: Rabbi Abba rescued R' Huna bar Chiyya’s tefillin.[^3] In [Shabbat 47a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.47a.6), too, we find the two together at Rav Huna’s doorway. Other colleagues were Levi bar Shmuel, as in [Sanhedrin 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.100a.4); Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiya and Rav Chilkiya bar Tuvya, as in [Gittin 57a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.57a.14); and Rav Hamnuna, as at the beginning of [Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.12.1.4). Rav Yosef was something of his pupil-colleague, as in [Bava Kamma 116b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.116b.21-22).

[Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6) tells a remarkable story about him.[^4] An occasion arose when Rav Huna bar Chiyya was needed—Rashi explains that the sages needed to ask him questions of law. Rav Yosef, Rabba, and four hundred pairs of scholars came to visit him. Hearing that they were coming, he prepared four hundred chairs for them. Subsequently, they heard that he had become a tax collector for the king. They sent him this message: “Let him go to his position of importance; let him return to his former standing!” He sent back, “I have withdrawn from it.” Rav Yosef did not go to him; Rabba did.[^5]

This illuminates what Rav Sherira Gaon writes in his Epistle, part 3, chapter 2: “We have heard from our scholars that, in those years after Rav Yehuda when Rabba did not accept the leadership, Rav Huna bar Chiyya presided in Pumbedita and had a large house of study there.”[^6]

The gaon R' Sh. Sh. raises an objection there against our master Rav Sherira, from [Gittin 60b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.60b.7): “That shofara”—the fund of the academy’s scholars, according to Rav Sherira—“was first in Rav Yehuda’s house, afterward in Rabba’s house,” and so forth. If R' Huna bar Chiyya presided in Pumbedita before Rabba, the Talmud should have mentioned him and said that, after Rav Yehuda, the fund was in R' Huna bar Chiyya’s house. That is the substance of his objection.[^7]

It is astonishing that a scholar of his stature should object on the basis of a Talmudic passage that Rav Sherira himself cites there! All Rav Sherira’s statements, however, are authentic received tradition. When Rav Yehuda died in Pumbedita, Rav Huna bar Chiyya was indeed the eldest among them. As we said above, he had been fortunate enough to receive teachings even from Shmuel; he was also the son-in-law of that generation’s eminent scholar, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, and exceedingly wealthy. To whom would the leadership be more fitting than to him?

That is the meaning of [Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6), where Rav Yosef, Rabba, and all the scholars went to him: he really had established a large house of study there, as Rav Sherira testifies. Had he not become a tax collector, he would undoubtedly have been head of the academy. But when they discovered that he was a tax collector, they withdrew from him. They then sent to the Land of Israel to ask whom they should appoint: Rav Yosef, who was “Sinai,” or Rabba, who was an “uprooter of mountains.”[^8] Rav Yosef, however, did not wish to accept the burden of the rabbinate. Rabba therefore had to accept that office: responsibility for directing and supporting the academy’s members. This is the meaning of the Talmud’s statement about the shofara.

This occurred immediately after Rav Yehuda’s death in the year 610. Rabba, who presided for twenty-two years, as explicitly stated at the end of [Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.64a.3-4) and [Horayot](https://www.sefaria.org/Horayot.14a.4), died in the year 632, as explicitly stated in Rav Sherira’s Epistle.[^9] Although Rabba began to preside immediately after Rav Yehuda, he did not accept formal authority as head of the academy, because Rav Chisda, the elder of the generation, then eighty-two years old, had succeeded Rav Huna at Sura. Rabba therefore went to Rav Chisda from time to time to resolve his doubts.

During that period, R' Huna bar Chiyya maintained a large house of study in Pumbedita, and Rabba sometimes visited him as well. Thus [Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6) explicitly says that, when Rav Huna bar Chiyya announced that he had withdrawn from tax collecting, Rabba went to him. Toward the end of Rav Chisda’s life—and perhaps R' Huna bar Chiyya had also died by then—Rabba became head of the generation. The Sura academy ceased to function after Rav Chisda’s death, and most of the scholars and of Israel were in Pumbedita. All this is set out briefly in Rav Sherira’s Epistle there.[^10]

Among his students we find Rav Acha, son of Rav Minyomin, who asked him a question in [Chullin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.80a.18).[^11] In [Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.2.5.3), Rabbi Yona reports a teaching in his name. He left a son distinguished in Torah, named Levi, as in [Shabbat 51b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.51b.18).

notes.text: Hyman expressly presents direct contact with Shmuel as a possibility. A report “in Shmuel’s name” does not, by itself, establish that its transmitter personally studied with him. Likewise, an attributed teaching is not automatically evidence of a direct teacher–student relationship.

The current Wikisource witness has ר״ג in two places in this discussion, although the interlocutor in Bava Batra 111a is Rav Nachman (ר״נ). The translation uses Rav Nachman. Without checking a facsimile, these discrepancies cannot be assigned specifically to Hyman’s printing rather than its transcription.

This translates Hyman’s account, rather than silently substituting the wording of a modern Talmud edition. The retrieved William Davidson Hebrew text of Moed Katan 26a relates the threatened swallowing and the discussion of garment-rending, but does not explicitly describe the rescue in Hyman’s terms. Hyman cites Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan, chapter 3, halakhah 4. The matching story is found at [3:7:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.7.11) in Sefaria’s Guggenheimer edition: an ostrich snatches Huna bar Chiyya’s tefillin, and Rabbi Abba catches and strangles it. The English body links the confirmed modern locator; Hyman’s supplied locator is retained here without assuming whether the discrepancy arose in printing, transcription or numbering.

The current Hebrew witness gives “Berakhot 31a” at the introduction to this story and again later in the historical argument. The story is in Bekhorot 31a. Wikisource’s own editorial footnote corrects the first occurrence; the English references point to Bekhorot.

The dismissive message is rendered as Hyman quotes it. Rashi explains “let him go to his importance” as telling him to pursue the important office he had chosen as a tax collector, while the sages would not visit him. The “four hundred pairs” and “four hundred chairs” are both retained from Hyman’s account.

The quoted tradition can be read in [Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon 1:98](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.98), in Sefaria’s *Seder HaChachamim*, Oxford, 1888 witness. Hyman’s part/chapter locator belongs to his cited arrangement; the link uses Sefaria’s current numbering.

The initials ר׳ ש״ש have been retained as “R' Sh. Sh.”; their expansion has not been established for this draft. “The academy scholars’ fund” is the interpretation of shofara that Hyman attributes to Rav Sherira, not an independently supplied literal translation of that term.

“Sinai” describes mastery of received learning; “uprooter of mountains” describes analytical power. The contrasting characterizations and the consultation with the Land of Israel appear in Berakhot 64a and Horayot 14a.

The years 610 and 632 are retained as Hyman gives them, in the Seleucid era. The independently retrieved Oxford 1888 witness of Rav Sherira’s Epistle instead gives Rabba’s death as 631 (תרל״א). The translation does not silently harmonize this difference or claim that Hyman consulted the same edition.

The preceding historical reconstruction, including the distinction between exercising leadership and accepting formal academy authority, is Hyman’s argument. His emphatic assertions and his qualification “perhaps” have both been preserved; they are not newly established historical conclusions.

The current Hyman transcription names Rav Acha son of Rav Minyomin. The retrieved William Davidson Hebrew witness of Chullin 80a:18 instead reads Abba son of Rav Minyomin bar Chiyya. Hyman’s naming is retained in the translation, with the difference recorded here rather than turned into an identity merge.

Titles are checked by occurrence. The cited Bavli passages explicitly use Rav Huna bar Chiyya, while the checked Yerushalmi Sheviit and Moed Katan passages use Rabbi Huna. The composite reporting formula and the abbreviated title in the Yerushalmi tefillin account therefore use neutral R', rather than harmonizing those witnesses. Rabbi Abba in the Shabbat and ostrich passages, and Rabbi Yona in Sheviit, have explicit title support in their corresponding named Hebrew passages. Hyman explicitly calls the father-in-law Rav Yirmeya bar Abba; Chullin 93a likewise has Rav, whereas the checked Shabbat 156a and Bava Kamma 59b passages have Rabbi Yirmeya. The Bava Kamma sentence follows its explicit title; the family prose retains Hyman’s full form. Unresolved titles in the cited scholar’s objection and Hyman’s tentative reconstruction remain R'. No title here establishes a historical identity.
